title: The shrewd manager (Luke 16:1–13)
hook: a puzzling story: use money to make friends; you can't serve two masters

segments.voice: Yesterday, teknon, the older brother, stood outside the party while his father pleaded. Your line was all I have is yours. Did you go in? Day five hundred sixty.

It may be the most puzzling story Jesus tells. Even Luke seems to feel the strain: after the story come four or five different morals, one after another. A dishonest employee gets praised. Money gets called unrighteous, then used to make friends. And it comes straight after the prodigal son, with a little clue linking them. The younger son wasted his father's goods. This manager, Luke says, is accused of wasting his master's goods. Same Greek word. Two stories about what we do with what isn't really ours.

A rich man's manager is caught wasting his goods and told to hand in the books. He panics, and in the King James Bible he talks to himself: "What shall I do? for my lord taketh away from me the stewardship: I cannot dig; to beg I am ashamed." Then he has an idea. He calls in his master's debtors one by one. How much do you owe? A hundred measures of oil. Quick, write fifty. And you? A hundred measures of wheat. Write eighty. Now when he's out of a job, they'll owe him a favor. And the punchline: "the lord commended the unjust steward, because he had done wisely." Not for being honest. For being shrewd, for seeing the crisis coming and acting fast. Scholars genuinely disagree about the details. Some think he cut out his own commission; others think he cut the master's interest; others that he was simply dishonest to the end. What's clear is the lesson Jesus draws: use the money of this world, mammon, to make friends, because people last and money doesn't. Mammon is an Aramaic word for wealth, and Jesus treats it almost like a rival god. Then the line that becomes today's carry: "He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much." Small things train big things. And the closing warning: "Ye cannot serve God and mammon." Money makes a fine servant and a terrible master. Look back at the week. Proverbs. A feast refused with excuses. A tower that needs counting. A grumble that started three stories. A son far off, and another at the door. And now a manager who at least saw clearly that his time was short.
screen: then, large: `FAITHFUL IN THAT WHICH IS LEAST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: use money to build a friendship. Settle and breathe. Think about the money that passed through your hands this week: rent, food, subscriptions, things you bought on a whim. Notice which of it made a connection with another person, and which didn't. Now think of one person you'd like to be closer to, or someone who could use a little help. What small amount could turn into a friendship? A coffee you pay for, a meal you share, a gift for no reason, covering someone's bus fare. Choose one. The bell holds the time.
Mammon, the Aramaic word for wealth, treated almost like a rival master — the shrewd manager's money, used to make friends instead of becoming the thing you serve.
Your line: faithful in little. Today, spend one small amount on a person instead of a thing. Day five hundred sixty, and another week on the path.

howItsDone: Christians use the language of stewardship for money, time and the earth, as things held in trust; many churches teach regular giving, and some Christians keep budgets that set aside money for hospitality and helping others.

match.prompt: what's inside Luke 16:1–13 — tap the pairs.
pairs: accused of wasting his master's goods
faithful in that which is least

myth: Jesus praises the manager for being dishonest
the master commends him for acting wisely, shrewdly, in a crisis. not for his honesty.
Luke uses the same word for wasted here and for the younger son
both waste what wasn't theirs: the son his father's, the manager his master's.
scholars all agree what the manager actually did
some say he cut his own commission, others the master's interest, others that he was simply dishonest.

fork.setup: you're a manager about to be fired. you can't dig and you're ashamed to beg. what do you do?
options: confess everything and hope for mercy.
cut what each debtor owes, so they'll welcome you later.
fork.reveal: he rewrites the bills, fifty for a hundred, eighty for a hundred, and the master commends him because he had done wisely.

original.note: Greek, from Aramaic: wealth, property. Jesus treats it almost like a rival master.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus approves of cooking the books.
what it means: be as clear-eyed about what lasts as this man was about his job, use money for people, and never let it be your master.
what a scholar hears: the verb for wasting links him to the prodigal, and scholars still debate whether he cut his commission, the interest, or simply cheated.
recall: the coin the KJV calls a farthing

notes: διασκορπίζω in Luke 15:13 and 16:1: confirm the shared verb.
The three readings (own commission, master's interest, plain dishonesty) are a standard summary of the debate. Confirm.
μαμωνᾶς from Aramaic māmōnā: standard lexicon.
'Money makes a fine servant and a terrible master' is a proverb, not scripture; spoken as commentary.

Audit (y2 10% sample): replaced stock hook lines ('you're in good company', 'scratched their heads') with a concrete observation that Luke follows the parable with a string of separate morals (16:8b-13); fixed the teach head 'make friends with it', which reversed Luke 16:9's sense (make friends by means of mammon). Keeper: confirm the description of 16:8b-13 as several appended sayings.
